common.tagline: Heat safety planning for coaches and band directors

footer.safetySummary: WBGT Check shows forecast-based remote estimates for planning. Remote estimates tend to read LOWER than on-site measurement — treat borderline readings as the higher category and confirm with an on-site WBGT meter before activity decisions. Your association's policy and your athletic trainer's judgment control.
footer.affiliation: wbgtcheck.com is an independent tool. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to the UIL, GHSA, NFHS, NATA, or any state athletic association.
footer.dataCredit: Weather data: NOAA / National Weather Service. WBGT model ported from ECMWF thermofeel (Apache-2.0).

guideline.discretion: Use discretion for intense or prolonged exercise; watch at-risk participants closely.
guideline.restBreaks: At least {{n}} separate rest breaks each hour, minimum {{minutes}} min each.
guideline.restBreaksRange: At least {{n}} separate rest/water breaks each hour, {{min}}–{{max}} min each.
guideline.restMinutes: At least {{minutes}} min of rest breaks distributed through each hour.
guideline.notAddressedBelow: The policy states no modifications below its lowest listed threshold.
guideline.tssaaFootballContactAllowed: Football: contact allowed and full pads may be worn for contact work, but shoulder pads and helmets come off for anything non-contact; all protective equipment except padded pants comes off for conditioning.
guideline.tssaaFootballNonContactNoEquipment: Football: no protective equipment for non-contact practice; it may be worn only for drills that do involve contact.
guideline.footballHelmetShoulderShorts: Football: helmet, shoulder pads and shorts only.
guideline.coolingZone: Mandatory on-site rapid cooling zone (tub or tarp).
guideline.noOutdoor: No outdoor workouts. Delay practice until a cooler WBGT is reached.

home.pageTitle: WBGT Forecast with State Heat Policy Flags
home.heroBadge: Free · No account · Nothing to install
home.intro: One screen for the morning call: hourly wet bulb globe temperature for your field, translated into your state's activity flags — rest ratios, equipment limits, practice caps — with a card you can drop in the team chat. Built for coaches, athletic trainers and marching band directors.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Enter a ZIP or tap the location button. We pull the National Weather Service hourly WBGT forecast for your exact grid cell; where NWS doesn't publish WBGT (parts of central Texas, for example) we model it from temperature, humidity, wind and cloud cover using the Liljegren method and mark it ESTIMATED. Then your selected policy — Texas UIL Class 2 or 3, Georgia GHSA, or the NATA example guideline — turns each hour into a flag.

sections.heading: Built to be conservative
sections.body: Field studies show remote WBGT estimates read about {{min}} °C low on average versus an on-site meter, and up to {{max}} °C low in the hottest conditions — the dangerous direction. WBGT Check flags borderline hours and tells you to plan for the higher category. A forecast plans the schedule; only an on-site reading runs the practice.

sections.heading: Use it the way trainers do
sections.body: Plan tomorrow's practice with the forecast the night before. Share the verdict card so every coach sees the same number and the same flag. Then run practice off your on-site reading, exactly as your policy writes it — this site plans and communicates; your instrument decides. Marching band directors work the same way: UIL's 2026-27 standard names marching band alongside athletics, and the hour-by-hour view is what tells you whether an after-school rehearsal block holds.

sections.heading: Know your state's rules
sections.body: Texas UIL explicitly accepts internet-based readings; Georgia GHSA requires a calibrated on-site instrument; other states fall everywhere in between. See the state-by-state table, the Texas UIL guide, and the Georgia GHSA guide for what your association actually requires.

verdict.estimatedExplain: NWS does not publish WBGT for this grid — value modeled (Liljegren) from temperature, humidity, wind and cloud cover.
verdict.conservativeNotice: Remote estimates read LOW vs on-site meters (−{{min}} to −{{max}} °C in studies). Near a boundary, treat it as the higher flag.
verdict.borderlineNotice: Within {{margin}} °F of the {{nextFlag}} boundary — plan for {{nextFlag}}.
verdict.verifyOnsite: Confirm on site before and during activity — this forecast is a planning aid, not a measurement.
verdict.surfaceNotice: Over dark tracks, hard courts, and sand, on-site readings can run higher than any remote estimate.
verdict.genericRegionNotice: The NATA example table was written for hot-climate regions. In northern states, New England, the Pacific coast, and high-altitude areas, lower thresholds may apply — local guidance takes precedence.
verdict.staleNotice: This forecast was loaded at {{time}} and may be out of date — refresh before making decisions.
verdict.deviceOnlyNotice: {{body}} requires an on-site, scientifically-approved WBGT instrument. This site's readings do NOT satisfy compliance — use them for planning only.
verdict.deviceRecommendedNotice: {{body}} calls for the reading to be taken on site — an on-site instrument is the named method. Use this forecast to plan, not as the reading you act on.
verdict.weekDrillHint: Each day shows its peak. Tap a day to see it hour by hour.
verdict.dayShowHours: Show this day hour by hour
verdict.noData: No forecast data for this period.
verdict.boundariesNote: Thresholds in °F WBGT, exactly as published by the source.
verdict.dataResolutionNote: Forecast values are NWS gridpoint data — one value for the grid cell around your point, not a reading at your exact field. Hours marked EST are modeled from temperature, humidity, wind and cloud cover (Liljegren method) where NWS publishes no WBGT.

measurement.uilTiming: UIL: read WBGT within {{before}} min before practice, then every {{interval}} min during.
measurement.uilApps: UIL's plan names "{{quote}}" as a method it accepts. It does not define "approved" or publish a list of approved internet resources, so whether this site can be your official reading is your district's call — plan with it, and confirm before relying on it as the reading.
measurement.ghsaTiming: GHSA: readings at least every {{interval}} min, beginning {{lead}} min before practice, from an on-site instrument.
measurement.ghsaCalibration: GHSA WBGT monitors must be calibrated at least every {{years}} years.

air.bothGatesNotice: Heat and air are two separate gates. Neither one clears the other — follow whichever is stricter.
air.pm25FallbackNotice: No PM2.5 reading for this area, so the overall AQI is standing in. Washington's table is written for PM2.5 — treat this verdict cautiously and check AirNow directly.

actions.healthCondsOptOut: Let students with health conditions opt out or stay indoors; limit their intensity if needed.
actions.healthCondsMove: Move students with health conditions somewhere with safer air — indoors or another location. Let everyone else opt out or stay indoors, and limit intensity.
actions.limitModerate: Limit outdoor activity to moderate intensity. Students with health conditions: limit further, or move them to safer air if needed.
actions.limitLightOrHourModerate: Limit to light intensity, or to one hour total at moderate intensity. If intensity and time cannot be modified, consider canceling — or move to safer air, indoors or another location.
actions.limitLightUnder4h: Limit to light intensity and under four hours total. If intensity and time cannot be modified, cancel — or move to safer air.
actions.cancelOrMoveFiltered: Cancel outdoor activity, or move it indoors with filtered air or to a different location. Keep indoor activity light if indoor PM2.5 is elevated.
actions.sensitiveConsiderIndoor: Athletes unusually sensitive to air pollution should consider indoor activity only. Rescue inhalers on hand, and pretreatment if their provider directs it. Anyone with respiratory illness, asthma, lung or heart disease watches symptoms and reduces or stops activity if they appear. Add rest periods as needed.
actions.addRestBreaksConsiderReschedule: All of the above, plus extra rest breaks for asthma, other lung disease, heart conditions or diabetes. Consider moving practice to another time or an area with a lower AQI, and weigh several days of elevated AQI together. Indoors may not be cleaner — check the ventilation.
actions.cancelOrMoveLowerAqi: All outdoor activity, practice and competition alike, shall be canceled or moved to an area with a lower AQI. Indoors may not be cleaner — check the ventilation.
actions.refrainOutdoor: No outdoor practice or competition. CIF member schools must refrain at or above this reading.

air.noPolicySummary: No verified state policy — EPA category only. Open for details.
air.noPolicyHeading: No verified policy for this state
air.noPolicyBody: We only carry air-quality practice rules we have read in the association's or health department's own document — Washington, Oregon and California so far. Everywhere else you get the EPA category and nothing more: ask your state association and your district what applies.
air.noActionStated: This source states no action at this level. That is not permission — it means the document is silent here.
air.areaFarNotice: The nearest monitor is about {{mi}} miles away. Smoke can differ sharply over that distance — use the 5-3-1 check and look at your own sky.
air.preliminaryNotice: Preliminary hourly reading. AirNow observations are not fully verified or validated and can change.
air.staleNotice: This reading is from {{time}} and may no longer describe the air outside.
air.notClearance: Planning input, not clearance to play. The person your school designates to monitor air quality decides, on site.
air.visibilityHeading: No monitor nearby? Use the 5-3-1 visibility check
air.visibilityBody: On a clear day, pick landmarks about {{near}}, {{mid}} and {{far}} miles from the field. Stand with the sun behind you: when a landmark's outline can no longer be seen, visibility is shorter than that distance.
air.visibilityRecheck: In smoke or haze, check the AQI or the visibility index at least hourly during practices and games — conditions turn over fast.
air.indoorWarning: Moving indoors is not automatically safer. If the ventilation cannot handle the smoke, indoor air may be worse than outside — and a gym runs hotter, so the heat gate still applies.
air.verifiedOn: Cross-checked against the primary document on {{date}}
air.loadFailed: Air quality is unavailable right now. Check AirNow directly before you decide.
air.dataSourcesHeading: Where the air number comes from
air.dataSourcesBody: Readings come from the EPA AirNow program, which republishes hourly observations from state, local and tribal air agencies. Credit belongs to those agencies first. Category colors follow the RGB values EPA specifies for the AQI, unaltered.

texas.intro: Starting {{effectiveDate}}, WBGT-based activity modification is a required standard for all UIL outdoor athletic activities — and marching band. Here is the policy in plain terms, with every number taken from UIL's published chart.
texas.classesBody: UIL assigns each county to a WBGT class on its regional map; hotter regions get higher (more permissive) thresholds because athletes there are more heat-acclimatized. Most of eastern and central Texas — including the Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin and San Antonio areas — falls under Class 3, while the Panhandle and far West Texas use Class 2. Find your county on the UIL map and select that class; this site defaults to the stricter Class 2 until you choose.
texas.measurementApps: UIL accepts internet-based readings: the plan permits a scientifically approved WBGT instrument "or other scientifically proven method, such as an internet-based weather station software or application." That makes forecast tools legitimate planning aids in Texas — but the reading that governs is the one taken at practice time.
texas.legalityHeading: Can this site be your official reading?
texas.legalityBody: The plan's requirement sentence names both lanes: "{{req}}" The FAQ says it even more directly: "{{faq}}"
texas.legalityNoList: What neither document provides: a definition of "approved" or a published list of approved internet resources. Whether a given forecast tool satisfies the standard is therefore your district's call — confirm with your district or athletic trainer before relying on any internet resource, this one included, as the official reading.
texas.mandate2026Body: UIL's own sentence: "{{quote}}" Marching band is named in the requirement itself, not implied.
texas.recordkeepingNote: Read the plan's verbs closely, because they change: the pre-practice reading must be taken within {{before}} minutes, while readings during practice should be taken every {{interval}} minutes — and keeping a written record is only recommended: "{{record}}" A written log is still the cheapest way to show you followed the cadence.
texas.internetCadenceNote: The plan does not treat the internet lane as a workaround. It gives that lane its own instructions, at the same cadence as a physical meter: "{{quote}}"
texas.linkedToolNote: One concrete signal about what UIL has in mind: the plan page links exactly one internet-based WBGT tool by name, the {{name}}, and no other. That is a link, not an approval — but it is the only worked example the plan itself points at.
texas.competitionNote: The activity chart governs practices. For competitions, a rapid cooling zone must still be on site and available at all times above threshold temperatures.
texas.bandNote: Marching band is covered: the UIL requirement applies to outdoor rehearsals, not just athletics.
texas.sourceBody: All thresholds and modification text above derive from the UIL Heat Stress & Athletic Participation plan and its WBGT Activity Guidelines chart, cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.

georgia.intro: GHSA By-law 2.67 requires WBGT-based practice modification in all sports during times of extremely high heat and humidity, and the by-law says the policy itself runs "{{yearRound}}" — this is not a football-season rule. Where Georgia is unusual is how it expects the reading to be taken.
georgia.deviceBody: The by-law's wording: "{{quote}}" Readings should be taken at least every {{interval}} minutes beginning {{lead}} minutes before practice, and monitors must be calibrated at least every {{years}} years.
georgia.holdBody: Once a reading has held a range for {{hold}} minutes, that range's restrictions apply for the rest of the practice — and they do not lift if the WBGT falls back. GHSA states it twice: "{{hold1}}" and "{{hold2}}" Going the other way is immediate: "{{escalate}}"
georgia.holdPlanning: For planning, that means the hottest range your practice window touches is the range you should staff and schedule for, not the range you start in.
georgia.seasonNote: Read that date limit carefully, because GHSA's two documents do not agree on it. The by-law attaches "(prior to October 1)" to its instrument sentence, while GHSA's own practice-policy reminder states the monitor requirement with no date limit at all. This site takes the stricter reading and treats Georgia as a device state all year. If you are planning after October 1, ask your athletic director which one your school is held to.
georgia.noAppsBody: GHSA has said it in as many words: "{{noApps}}" And the same reminder leaves no room for a practice without a device: "{{monitor}}"
georgia.deviceWarning: App and web estimates — including this site — are NOT accepted for GHSA compliance. Use WBGT Check to plan tomorrow's schedule; use your calibrated on-site meter to run practice.
georgia.practiceDefBody: Practice time runs from when players report to the practice area until they leave it. Conditioning (weights, sprints, timed runs) counts as practice time — including "voluntary" workouts. Walk-throughs are separate: max one hour, no equipment, no conditioning, no contact.
georgia.sourceBody: All thresholds and modification text above derive from GHSA By-law 2.67 (Practice Policy for Heat and Humidity), cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.

wbgtVsHi.pageTitle: WBGT vs Heat Index (vs Wet Bulb)
wbgtVsHi.intro: Three different numbers get called "wet bulb" in team group chats, and mixing them up leads to bad practice decisions. Here is what each one actually measures.
wbgtVsHi.wbgtBody: A weighted composite built for people exerting themselves outdoors: 70% natural wet bulb (evaporative cooling power), 20% black globe (solar radiation load), 10% dry air temperature. Wind, sun, humidity and heat all move it. Sports heat policies (UIL, GHSA, NCAA, the military) are written against WBGT.
wbgtVsHi.wetbulbHeading: Plain wet bulb is not WBGT
wbgtVsHi.wetbulbBody: The plain (psychrometric) wet bulb only captures evaporation — no sun load. On a sunny field, WBGT runs well above plain wet bulb. If your weather app shows "wet bulb 78°" on a cloudless afternoon, the WBGT on the turf can already be in flag territory.
wbgtVsHi.hiHeading: Heat index — a different scale entirely
wbgtVsHi.hiBody: Heat index models how hot it feels to a person at rest in the shade, in normal clothes. It has little relevance to a football practice. The scales do not line up: per GHSA's own FAQ, a WBGT of {{wbgtExample}} is roughly comparable to a heat index of {{hiExampleRange}}.
wbgtVsHi.hiNote: Some states (e.g. New York) write their policies against heat index instead — that is a policy choice, not an equivalence. Never read a WBGT threshold with a heat index number, or vice versa.

states.intro: No public roster classifies how each state lets you MEASURE WBGT — so we built one. Three buckets: apps and web readings accepted, on-site device required, or not specified by the association. Rows marked as primary-source verified were read against the association's or legislature's own document and date-stamped; the rest come from our research pass and deserve a call to your association before you rely on them. One more layer: your school district or county school system may impose stricter rules than the state association — in Virginia and Maryland, districts set thresholds by law.
states.legendApps: Apps allowed — the association explicitly accepts internet/app-based readings.
states.legendDevice: Device only — an on-site scientifically-approved instrument is mandated; app/web readings do not satisfy the policy.
states.legendUnverified: Not specified / unverified — confirm with the association.

notes.tx: Effective {{effectiveDate}}; covers athletics and marching band. Class 2/3 regional thresholds — see the Texas guide. Internet WBGT resources are explicitly allowed; no approval list is published.
notes.ga: On-site calibrated instrument required at each practice — see the Georgia guide.
notes.ky: KHSAA moved to WBGT and is reported to rule out websites and phone apps as substitutes — we could not reach the KHSAA documents to confirm the wording or which record form governs. Confirm directly.
notes.sc: Schools are required to own and use an on-site WBGT thermometer; "phone apps are not scientifically approved". Range-hold rule locks in restrictions — see the South Carolina guide.
notes.ia: WBGT is recommended (not mandated) year-round above 80 °F, readings every 30 minutes; marching band and cheer have their own rows — see the Iowa guide.
notes.fl: Zachary Martin Act legislates WBGT-based safety requirements; FHSAA operates on WBGT.
notes.nc: Current handbook calls for a scientifically approved device, read hourly from 30 minutes before practice; §2.3.3(g) makes the containing policy mandatory. Stricter threshold family than most states — see the North Carolina guide.
notes.va: Code §22.1-271.10 (2025) requires every school board to adopt WBGT-based policies with at least five tiers, but districts set the thresholds; measurement method not regulated — see the Virginia guide.
notes.tn: Each school reads either WBGT or heat index; a phone app is permitted for heat index only, as a last resort. Marching band not covered — see the Tennessee guide.
notes.mo: MSHSAA: WBGT must be utilized above 80 °F air temperature (2025 update); field-oriented wording.
notes.md: MPSSAA delegates to district policies; WBGT and heat index both appear.
notes.ny: NYSPHSAA works from heat index, not WBGT, and directs schools to read it from a named weather app by ZIP code — see the New York guide.
notes.ca: AB 1653 orders CIF to set a standard; details pending.

states.caveat: This table is a navigation aid, not legal advice. Policies change midseason; the association's current document controls. Found an error? Tell your athletic trainer first, then us.

southCarolina.intro: South Carolina is one of the strictest states on how you get the number: the League requires every school to own and use an on-site WBGT thermometer, and says in writing that phone apps do not count.
southCarolina.deviceHeading: South Carolina is a device-only state
southCarolina.deviceBody: The guidelines open with a requirement, not a suggestion: "{{required}}". On measurement they add: "{{device}}" And explicitly: "{{apps}}"
southCarolina.deviceWarning: App and web estimates — including this site — are NOT accepted for SCHSL compliance. Plan tomorrow's schedule here; run today's practice off your calibrated on-site meter.
southCarolina.measurementTiming: Readings are taken directly on the playing surface {{lead}} minutes before activity and every {{interval}} minutes after.
southCarolina.measurementHold: The range-hold rule is unusual and worth knowing: once a reading has stayed in a range for {{hold}} minutes, that range's restrictions lock in and cannot be relaxed to a lower range. Time already spent does not carry over into a new category.
southCarolina.measurementCalibration: WBGT devices must be recalibrated every {{years}} years, or sooner if the manufacturer says so.
southCarolina.immersionNote: Cold immersion has its own trigger: from WBGT {{immersion}} upward, a cold immersion tub or equivalent water-based cooling must be immediately available — supplies ready to use, not merely owned.
southCarolina.continuousNote: The red band has a sentence cross-country coaches should read twice: "{{quote}}" If your event cannot take the prescribed breaks, the remedy is delay or cancellation, not shorter breaks.
southCarolina.sourceBody: All thresholds and modification text above derive from the SCHSL Heat and Acclimatization Guidelines, cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.
southCarolina.boundaryNote: One wrinkle in the source: the table prints the top band as "{{tableLabel}}" while the text elsewhere says "{{textLabel}}". This site resolves that gap upward — the hotter category — so a reading in between is treated as the black flag.

iowa.boundaryNote: One boundary quirk: the table prints "{{tableLow}}" and then "{{tableNext}}", leaving the boundary value itself unassigned. This site resolves that gap upward — it reads as the yellow flag.
iowa.intro: Iowa is the state that remembered the band. Its WBGT guidance is issued jointly by the two athletic associations and the music and speech associations, so marching band and cheerleading get their own modification rows instead of being left to guess.
iowa.recommendedHeading: Recommended, not mandated — read the wording carefully
iowa.recommendedBody: Iowa's document approves WBGT as "the recommended measurement practice and device", and says: "{{recommended}}" That is guidance, not a mandate, and this site says so rather than overstating it. Your conference or district may still require it.
iowa.categoryBody: The thresholds below are Iowa's, and they apply statewide: the associations state that "Category {{category}} is where Iowa is at and how we derived our numbers for our policy." Those Category {{category}} boundaries are the same set Texas uses for its Class 2 counties — the same national region system, reached independently.
iowa.appsHeading: Iowa tells you not to use a weather app
iowa.appsBody: From the associations' own FAQ: "{{apps}}" That is the honest case against using a tool like this one as your reading — a forecast cannot see your turf, your shade, or your stadium bowl.
iowa.measurementHeading: How Iowa says to take the reading
iowa.measurementBody: Set the device up at the venue {{accMin}}–{{accMax}} minutes ahead so it can acclimatize, {{height}} feet off the ground, away from obstructions, in the sun — and on the turf if that is where you are practising. Then read it every {{interval}} minutes, with the same person monitoring throughout.
iowa.bandBody: Iowa's appendix gives band and cheer their own rules: at the orange band, half uniform only — no long sleeves or long pants — and move practice onto grass rather than turf or concrete. At the red band, out of uniform: shorts, t-shirts and footwear only, and no conditioning. At the black band, outdoor activity stops.
iowa.triggerNote: The guidance applies year-round whenever ambient air temperature is above {{trigger}} °F — indoors or outdoors. A hot gym counts.
iowa.sourceBody: All thresholds and modification text above derive from the joint IHSAA / IGHSAU / IHSMA / IHSSA WBGT Heat Modification Guidance, cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.

tennessee.intro: Tennessee is the clearest example of a state that lets you pick your instrument. Each school reads either WBGT or heat index — and the two ladders are printed side by side, so the same practice can be governed by two different numbers depending on what you own.
tennessee.choiceHeading: WBGT or heat index — the school chooses
tennessee.choiceBody: The policy's first line: "{{either}}" It then puts a thumb on the scale: "{{firstChoice}}"
tennessee.appsHeading: When a phone app is allowed
tennessee.appsBody: Tennessee is unusual in permitting an app in writing — but only for heat index, and only as a last resort: "{{apps}}" Note what that does not say. It does not authorise a phone or a website as your WBGT reading; the policy asks for a reading "at the site" of the activity.
tennessee.hiTableHeading: The heat index ladder it pairs with
tennessee.hiTableNote: These are heat index degrees, not WBGT. The pairing below is TSSAA's own — it is a policy choice about which number triggers which rule, not a claim that the two scales are equivalent.
tennessee.lowBandNote: The policy's table starts at its lowest listed threshold and states nothing below it. This site shows that silence instead of inventing a "normal activities" row.
tennessee.coldTubHeading: Cold water immersion — for every warm-weather practice
tennessee.coldTubBody: This recommendation is not tied to any band; the policy bolds it as a baseline for all of them: "{{quote}}"
tennessee.scopeBody: The policy is written for practices and interscholastic competitions, including preseason scrimmages and jamborees. It does not mention marching band, so band directors in Tennessee have no state rule to point at — ask your district.
tennessee.sourceBody: All thresholds and modification text above derive from the TSSAA Heat Policy (revised {{revision}}), cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.

northCarolina.intro: North Carolina's activity chart starts stricter than most states' and escalates through four steps to full suspension at 90 °F WBGT. This page follows the current handbook — which keeps the familiar thresholds and quietly drops several clauses older copies still circulate.
northCarolina.measurementBody: The current handbook's wording: "{{device}}" It continues: "{{cadence}}" Earlier editions allowed a weather-station or airport reading within a few miles of the field; the current handbook contains no such clause. Treat an on-field device as the standard, and anything remote — including this site — as planning input only.
northCarolina.pickerExclusionHeading: Why North Carolina is not in the policy picker
northCarolina.pickerExclusionBody: NCHSAA's thresholds are a different family from this site's flag bands (80/85/88/90 versus 82/87/90/92 °F). Wiring them into the flag scale would print a verdict the association's own chart contradicts, so this page shows NCHSAA's chart in its own two columns and North Carolina stays deliberately absent from the forecast tool's policy picker. Older editions also printed a five-colour code next to the chart; the current handbook does not.
northCarolina.tableHeading: NCHSAA WBGT Index and Athletic Activity Chart

rows.unlimited: Unlimited activity, with primary cautions for new or unconditioned athletes and for extreme exertion.
rows.normal: Normal practice; closely monitor new or unconditioned athletes, and all athletes during extreme exertion.
rows.reducedIntensity: New or unconditioned athletes should have reduced-intensity practice and modifications in clothing. Well-conditioned athletes should have more frequent rest breaks and hydration, with cautious monitoring for heat illness symptoms.
rows.observation: All athletes must be under constant observation and supervision.
rows.immersion: Have a cold or ice immersion pool on site for practice.
rows.suspend: Suspend all practices. Competition may continue with mandatory water breaks as designated by the gameday administrator.

northCarolina.mandateBody: The chart's own verbs are mostly "should" — but the handbook's health and safety section is explicit about the policy that contains them: "{{mandate}}" Read the chart as the content of a policy your school is required to follow, and confirm the current handbook language with the NCHSAA before relying on it.
northCarolina.sourceBody: The chart and quotations above come from the 2025-26 NCHSAA Handbook (§2.3.5 Prevention of Heat Illness and §2.3.3), cross-checked against the current print edition on {{verifiedOn}}.

newYork.intro: New York is the state that shows WBGT is a choice, not a law of nature. Its procedure is written against heat index, and it tells schools to read that number from a phone app by ZIP code — the exact thing Georgia, South Carolina and Iowa warn against.
newYork.notWbgtHeading: This is a heat index policy
newYork.notWbgtBody: The procedure checks "Feels Like" temperature — heat index — {{lead}} hour before the contest or practice whenever air temperature is {{trigger}} °F or higher. A WBGT indicator is offered as an alternative, but heat index is the ladder the thresholds are written for.
newYork.appBody: In writing: "{{app}}" and "{{zip}}" A remote, ZIP-code-level reading is not a workaround in New York — it is the documented procedure.
newYork.appCaveat: That does not make a remote reading physically accurate; it makes it permitted. Everything this site says about remote estimates reading low still applies, and a heat index number cannot be compared against a WBGT threshold in either direction.

rows.water: Provide ample water and multiple water breaks; monitor athletes for heat illness.
rows.considerShorten: Consider reducing the length of the practice session.
rows.considerPostpone: Consider postponing practice to a time when the Feels Like temperature is lower.
rows.considerPostponeMuch: Consider postponing practice to a time when the Feels Like temperature is much lower.
rows.recovery: One hour of recovery time for every hour of practice.
rows.breaks15: Provide ample water and water breaks every {{minutes}} minutes.
rows.clothing: Light weight, loose fitting clothes should be worn.
rows.helmetsOnly: For practices, football helmets only — no other protective equipment.
rows.noOutside: No outside activity, practice or contest, should be held. Indoor activity only if air conditioned.

newYork.wbgtChartNote: New York does publish a WBGT alternative chart, but its thresholds depend on a regional category looked up from an external map, and the chart itself was not machine-readable in the source document. This site does not reproduce New York WBGT numbers rather than risk printing the wrong region's.
newYork.sourceBody: The thresholds and quotations above come from the NYSPHSAA Heat Index Procedures (approved {{approved}}, updated {{updated}}), cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}.

virginia.pageTitle: Virginia's Heat Law: Your District Sets the Numbers
virginia.intro: Virginia has a statute, not a threshold table. A 2025 law makes heat policy mandatory for every school board in the Commonwealth — and then leaves the actual WBGT levels to each district, which is why no honest page can tell you Virginia's cancellation number.
virginia.statuteBody: Code of Virginia {{section}} ({{citation}}) directs the Board of Education to develop and biennially review heat guidelines, and then requires each school board to adopt its own policies in line with them.
virginia.districtBody: The law tells districts what their policy must contain, not what the numbers are. District policies must "{{cancel}}" — so the WBGT level at which your practice is cancelled is a decision your school board made, and the only place to read it is your division's own policy.
virginia.consistencyBody: District policies must also "{{consistency}}" — in practice, the VHSL's WBGT-based guidance. VHSL's own rule is advisory; the statute is what makes a local policy mandatory.
virginia.tiersBody: Every district policy must include a heat-acclimatization and modification procedure with at least {{tiers}} tiers, escalating from the mildest level needing precautions up to the level at which activity is cancelled — covering equipment modification, work-to-rest ratios, water breaks and shaded rest.
virginia.iceHeading: The one number in the statute
virginia.iceBody: The statute fixes exactly one WBGT threshold, and it is about supplies rather than activity: ice must be provided to every student-athlete and every coach any time WBGT is {{ice}} °F or higher. Athletes must also have unhindered access at all times to hydration and a cooling space — shaded or air-conditioned.
virginia.measurementBody: The statute says nothing about how WBGT is measured — no device requirement, no rule about apps or websites. That silence is not permission: your district's policy may impose one, and it controls.
virginia.reportingBody: Districts must also establish a process for reporting and investigating any case where a student-athlete suffers a severe heat-related illness requiring emergency treatment or resulting in death.
virginia.noTableNotice: This page has no threshold table on purpose. Virginia's numbers live in local school board policy, and inventing a statewide table — or copying another state's — would be the exact failure this site exists to avoid.
virginia.sourceBody: The requirements and quotations above come from the text of Code of Virginia {{section}}, cross-checked on {{verifiedOn}}. The effective date is not printed on the code page — confirm it, and your district's thresholds, locally.

washingtonAir.pageTitle: Washington school air quality: cancel or move practice?
washingtonAir.intro: Washington's health department keys its air-quality guidance to how long children are outside — 15 minutes to an hour, one to four hours, or longer — because duration changes what the same reading demands. This page carries the current guide's table as printed, alongside the reading for your field.
washingtonAir.basisHeading: It is keyed to PM2.5, not the overall AQI
washingtonAir.basisBody: The table is headed "Outside Air Quality Index (AQI): PM2.5", so its thresholds follow the PM2.5 sub-index. The overall AQI can be driven by ozone instead, and on a smoky day the two can differ — so the forecast page shows you both numbers.
washingtonAir.dataSourceBody: The guide's own pointer for readings is the same feed this site's air gate uses: "{{quote}}"
washingtonAir.sensitiveGroupHeading: Who counts as a sensitive group here
washingtonAir.sensitiveGroupBody: In this guide, everyone on your roster: "{{quote}}" Rows that mention health conditions add further limits on top of that baseline.
washingtonAir.athleticsNote: The 1–4 hour column is the one most coaches and band directors need — it is where the guide itself files athletic events and practices, and its actions tighten a step sooner than the shortest column at the same reading.
washingtonAir.sourceBody: Every threshold and action on this page was read off the primary document.

oregonAir.pageTitle: Oregon OSAA air quality rules for practices and contests
oregonAir.intro: OSAA's air quality guidelines set required actions by AQI band, and they are the only source we verified that also publishes an AQI-to-visibility mapping — which matters when the nearest monitor sits far from your field.
oregonAir.belowRangeBody: The chart starts at its moderate band. OSAA states no action below that, and we will not invent one — a silent document is not a clearance.
oregonAir.conservativeBody: OSAA's own instruction when readings differ: "{{quote}}"
oregonAir.sourceBody: Every threshold and action on this page was read off the primary document.

californiaAir.pageTitle: California CIF air quality bylaw: the outdoor practice threshold
californiaAir.intro: California's rule is a single hard line rather than graduated guidance. At or above one reading, CIF member schools must stop outdoor practice and competition; below it the bylaw says nothing at all.
californiaAir.ruleBody: The bylaw's operative sentence, in full: "{{quote}}"
californiaAir.readingsBody: The same bylaw names its acceptable sources: "{{quote}}"
californiaAir.readingsNote: That sentence is why this site's air gate reads AirNow: the bylaw names it as an acceptable source. It still does not make a website the decision-maker — your designated monitor is.
californiaAir.belowBody: The bylaw is silent below that reading. Your section, district or local health department may set something stricter, and the heat gate is unaffected either way.
californiaAir.sourceBody: Every threshold and quotation on this page was read off the primary document.

disclaimerPage.notMeasurement: WBGT Check is a forecast-based planning aid. It is not a measuring instrument, and its numbers are not measurements. On-site WBGT at your field can differ substantially from any remote estimate — published comparisons found remote values roughly {{min}} °C low on average, and up to {{max}} °C low in the most dangerous conditions, which is the unsafe direction.
disclaimerPage.notCompliance: This site does not satisfy any association's measurement requirement in states that mandate an on-site instrument (e.g. Georgia GHSA, Kentucky KHSAA). Where internet-based readings are accepted (e.g. Texas UIL), the governing reading is still the one taken at the required time and place under the association's rules.
disclaimerPage.notMedical: Nothing here is medical advice. Heat illness decisions belong to qualified medical personnel — athletic trainers, team physicians, EMS. If someone shows signs of exertional heat stroke, call emergency services and begin rapid cooling immediately; do not consult a website. This service is not intended to serve as a primary emergency warning system, nor for emergency or life-safety decisions.
disclaimerPage.conditions: Conditions change during a session. A morning forecast cannot govern an afternoon practice; re-check and re-measure at the intervals your policy requires. Pay attention to the date and time of the data displayed — a verdict is only as current as the forecast it was loaded from.
disclaimerPage.airQuality: Air quality on this site is a preliminary hourly reading for an entire reporting area — not a measurement at your field. AirNow observations are not fully verified or validated and are subject to change, they refresh about once an hour, and the nearest monitor can be many miles away, so smoke may be far worse or far better where you are standing. EPA states these data should not be used to act as guidance or to support public decision-making. Treat the air gate as one input to an on-site judgment made by the person your school designates, alongside the 5-3-1 visibility check. Air quality never lowers a heat flag: where both gates apply, the stricter one does.
disclaimerPage.availability: This service depends on data from the National Weather Service, which itself makes no guarantee that its data reaches the internet on time or at all — and neither do we. We do not warrant that this service will be uninterrupted, timely, or error-free; it may be unavailable, delayed, or wrong precisely when conditions are most dangerous. Always have an on-site measurement plan that does not depend on this tool.
disclaimerPage.accuracy: We cross-check policy numbers against association primary documents and date-stamp each verification, but associations revise policies without notice. The association's current published document always controls over anything shown here.
disclaimerPage.liability: This service is provided "AS IS" and "as available", without warranties of any kind, express or implied, including the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. To the maximum extent permitted by law, WBGT Check and its operator shall not be liable for personal injury, death, or property damage, nor for any indirect, incidental, consequential, special, or punitive damages, arising from use of or reliance on this service. This service is not a substitute for independent judgment, additional safety measures, or common sense.
disclaimerPage.governingLaw: These terms and any dispute arising from this service are governed by the laws of the Republic of Korea, without regard to conflict-of-law rules. The Seoul Central District Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction as the court of first instance.

privacy.intro: WBGT Check is built to need as little of your data as possible.
privacy.locationContent: ZIP codes and geolocation coordinates are used only to fetch a forecast for that point. A ZIP you type goes to the lookup service (zippopotam.us); the coordinates go to our forecast proxy, which passes them to NOAA. Neither is stored server-side. Your last location is saved in your browser's localStorage so the verdict loads instantly next time; clear it with your browser data.
privacy.logContent: The reading log never leaves your device. Each entry holds the time, the WBGT, whether it came from the forecast or from your own meter, the flag and policy it was read against, and the location label you had set at the time. Up to {{max}} entries are kept in your browser's localStorage with no expiry — we never receive them, and nothing is sent anywhere when you save one. "Clear all" on the log deletes every entry immediately, and clearing your browser data removes them too.
privacy.storageTitle: What else this site stores on your device
privacy.storageContent: Also in localStorage: your last location, your chosen policy and — in Texas — your UIL class, your light or dark preference, the activity duration the air-quality table uses, and a flag recording that you dismissed the add-to-home-screen hint. One value in session storage keeps a failed update from reloading in a loop. None of it is sent to us, and all of it clears with your browser data. If your browser blocks storage entirely, the site still works; it just forgets these between visits.
privacy.analyticsContent: We use Google Analytics 4 to understand aggregate usage (which pages are read, whether the share card is used). GA4 sets cookies; in EEA/UK regions consent defaults to denied. We do not run ads on this site today.
privacy.dataContent: Forecast data comes from NOAA's National Weather Service API, requested through our server proxy with only the coordinates being asked about. Air-quality observations come from AirNow, run by the US EPA and partner agencies. Air quality works differently on purpose: our server downloads AirNow's whole hourly observation file and finds the nearest reporting area itself, so your coordinates are never sent to AirNow or the EPA.

notFound.title: Page not found
notFound.body: That page doesn't exist. Check the address, or head to the forecast.
